title: How Hong Kong connected
deck: A four-decade view of internet adoption—and a reminder that subscriptions and people are not the same measure.
question: How did internet access change in Hong Kong, and how do user counts compare with cellular and broadband subscriptions?
method: I filtered the global country-year dataset to Hong Kong, then followed internet-user counts and three access indicators over time with line charts.
finding: The series shows a strong rise in internet use from the mid-1990s onward. Cellular subscriptions grow on a different scale and eventually exceed 100 per 100 people, so they cannot be read as a count of unique internet users.
limitation: These are aggregated country-level indicators. A subscription is not proof that a unique person has internet access, and the dataset’s definitions should be checked before comparing metrics directly.

charts.caption: Internet-user counts rise markedly after the mid-1990s.

charts.alt: Line chart comparing internet use, cellular subscriptions, and broadband subscriptions in Hong Kong.
charts.caption: Comparing indicators reveals that subscriptions and internet users measure different things.

steps.title: Start wide
steps.text: The source dataset spans countries and years. I first checked its size and fields before narrowing the question to one place.

steps.title: Filter to Hong Kong
steps.text: The project uses the Hong Kong time series, keeping the country filter explicit so the plotted trend has a clear scope.

steps.title: Compare carefully
steps.text: Separate charts make the change over time visible while preserving the distinction between internet users and service subscriptions.

reflection: A useful next step would be to verify indicator definitions and add population-normalized measures before making direct cross-metric comparisons.

title: A decision tree on a 61-row loan sample
deck: A small classification exercise that produced a high holdout score—and a clear lesson about sample size and model validation.
question: Can applicant attributes help a decision tree distinguish the recorded approved and denied loan outcomes?
method: I one-hot encoded the non-target columns, split the 61 rows 50/50, fit a default DecisionTreeClassifier, and reviewed accuracy, a classification report, and a confusion matrix.
finding: The saved run scored 30 of 31 test records correctly (96.8%). The confusion matrix shows 19 approved records classified correctly, one approved record misclassified, and all 11 denied records classified correctly in that split.
limitation: This is not evidence of real-world lending performance. The dataset is tiny, one-hot encoding expands it to 147 features, and the split has no fixed random seed. The result can change substantially with a different split; fairness, calibration, and external validation were not assessed.
dataFiles: loan.csv (61 rows; source described on the original project page as Kaggle)

charts.caption: The sample contains more approved than denied outcomes.

charts.alt: Confusion matrix for the saved decision-tree test split.
charts.caption: The matrix makes the single misclassified test record visible.

charts.alt: Decision tree produced by the original notebook.
charts.caption: The original tree is included as a record of the model, not as a recommended decision policy.

steps.title: Inspect the sample
steps.text: The notebook checks fields, types, missingness, and outcome counts before preparing model inputs.

steps.title: Encode and split
steps.text: Categorical and numeric columns are one-hot encoded. A single 50/50 train-test split leaves only 31 records for evaluation.

steps.title: Evaluate the errors
steps.text: Accuracy is paired with class-level precision and recall and a confusion matrix, which is more informative than a score alone.

reflection: For a stronger study, I would use stratified cross-validation, prune or regularize the tree, compare simple baselines, and test error rates across relevant groups. This model should never be used to make actual credit decisions.

title: When weather meets produce prices
deck: Joining UK weather and weekly produce-price records to test whether a few weather variables explain price movement.
question: Do temperature, humidity, or wind speed help explain weekly fruit and vegetable prices in the UK?
method: I converted weather records to weekly observations, aligned dates, joined them with produce prices, then tested K-nearest-neighbor and linear-regression models on selected products and weather features.
finding: Weather alone was a weak predictor for apples in the saved runs (R² around 0.02–0.04). Carrot prices had a stronger relationship with temperature in one model (R² 0.33), while humidity was weaker (0.13) and wind speed offered little explanatory value. These are exploratory associations, not causal effects.
limitation: The two sources have different collection frequencies and are aligned through sampled dates. The simple models omit many potential drivers of price; an apparent change after 2020 cannot be attributed to COVID-19 from this analysis alone.
dataFiles: combined_united_kingdom_2017_to_2022.csv (weather source noted as Visual Crossing)

steps.title: Align the timelines
steps.text: Price data is weekly while weather data is daily. The notebook samples the weather series by week and joins on matching dates.

steps.title: Fit simple baselines
steps.text: KNN is used for a pear-price exercise; linear regression tests temperature, humidity, and wind speed for selected products.

steps.title: Read the score with context
steps.text: R² and mean squared error are useful diagnostics, but they do not show that weather causes the price changes.

reflection: A stronger model would use a time-aware validation split and add seasonality, variety, supply, and market variables. I would also report uncertainty and compare against a time-series baseline.

title: Exploring customer segments
deck: Using scaling, PCA, and K-means to explore patterns in customer purchasing and campaign-response data.
question: Can purchasing and engagement patterns be grouped into a small number of customer segments?
method: The notebook removes Education and Marital_Status, standardizes numeric columns, uses PCA and an elbow/silhouette review to explore cluster counts, then fits K-means with three clusters.
finding: After rows with missing values are dropped, 2,216 records remain. The selected three-cluster run contains groups of 1,040, 635, and 541 records. Correlation and cluster-profile plots help inspect patterns; the notebook does not establish a validated customer strategy.
limitation: The analysis omits two categorical fields, includes ID among standardized numeric features, and drops 24 rows with missing values. Those choices can affect distance-based clusters. The three groups need further validation and substantive interpretation before being used for business decisions.

steps.title: Prepare numeric features
steps.text: The notebook removes two categorical fields, checks missingness, standardizes numeric columns, and excludes incomplete rows before PCA and clustering.

steps.title: Explore the structure
steps.text: A three-component PCA view and elbow/silhouette diagnostics are used to examine candidate groupings.

steps.title: Inspect the segments
steps.text: K-means with three clusters yields groups of 1,040, 635, and 541 records, then boxplots compare standardized features.

reflection: I would exclude identifier columns, encode categorical variables deliberately, compare cluster stability across seeds, and validate any proposed segment against outcomes not used to create it.
